title: Mechanical Camel
subject: Contracts
stem:
Pass-1 Step 1 — black-letter rule being tested.
A contract may be rescinded for mistake when the mistaken fact existed at contracting, went to a basic assumption of the bargain, materially harmed the party seeking rescission, and was not a risk that party bore.

Pass-1 Step 2 — invariant layer preserved.
The issue remains buyer-side rescission for mistake. The credited outcome remains the hidden, undiscoverable, main-use defect. The dominant trap remains the pedigree/authenticity paperwork mistake. The call remains a “which scenario best supports buyer rather than seller rescission” call. The answer-array geometry remains a 3-vs-1 scenario set: three post-sale surprises fail because they do not support buyer-side mistake rescission; one hidden main-use defect survives.

Pass-1 Step 5 — locked final Christian variation.

Mary, who knew nothing about stage machinery, inherited a motorized camel prop from her late uncle’s attic. The camel had an annoying habit of jerking and startling children during rehearsals. Mary sold the camel for $2,400 to Daniel, an experienced designer of touring Christmas pageants, who knew that Mary was ignorant about stage machinery. Before the sale, Mary told Daniel, “I hate to say it, but this camel jerks around and is nothing special.”

Which one of the following scenarios would best support an action by Daniel, rather than Mary, to rescind the sale?
call: Which one of the following scenarios would best support an action by Daniel, rather than Mary, to rescind the sale?

choices.A: After the camel had completed four Advent tours for Daniel, it was discovered that, because of a clerical error unknown to both parties, the maker’s certificate listed an obscure prop shop as the builder rather than the famous Jerusalem Stageworks workshop that had actually built it.
choices.B: A week after the sale, while Daniel was testing the camel, it suddenly jerked, threw him from its platform, and injured him so severely that he was hospitalized for seven months and needed eighteen months for full recovery.
choices.C: In its debut pageant after the sale, the camel rolled smoothly to the center mark but shut down permanently during the final scene because of a rare internal crack in the main drive shaft that was undiscoverable except by complete disassembly.
choices.D: The camel earned Daniel $4.8 million over a four-year touring career, but when retired it was found to have nonstandard internal electronics and to be useless as a template for manufacturing replica camels.

rightExplanation:
C is correct. Daniel’s best rescission scenario is the hidden internal crack. The defect existed at the time of sale, could not be found without complete disassembly, and destroyed the camel’s core expected use in its debut pageant.

Gold Key: A mistake supports rescission only when the mistaken fact existed at contracting, went to a basic assumption with material adverse effect, and the party seeking rescission did not bear that risk. The hidden drive-shaft crack fits that pattern. Silver Key: On a buyer-rather-than-seller rescission call, sort each scenario by direction and purpose. C is the only scenario where the buyer is harmed by a hidden defect that defeats the main bargain.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text:
Signal: the certificate fact points away from Daniel’s rescission claim. Famous actual maker means hidden upside, not buyer harm.
Label: NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element.
Result: cut after the Silver Key direction check.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text:
Signal: the later injury matches the disclosed jerking trait.
Label: NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element.
Result: cut after the Gold Key known-risk check.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text:
Signal: the camel earned value for four years before the side-use defect appeared.
Label: NOT_RESPONSIVE / wrong_element.
Result: cut after the Gold Key main-use versus side-use check.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: C remains. It is buyer-harming, hidden, existing, main-use destroying, and not the disclosed jerking risk.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: No structural tiebreaker is needed after the Gold Key-assisted cut.

studentScript: The call asks for Daniel's rescission case. A helps Daniel or Mary, B is the warned-about jerking risk, and D is a side-use problem after the camel already earned money. C is the hidden defect that kills the main use, so C.

A.signal: The actual maker is better than the listed maker; that does not hurt Daniel.
A.lawyer: This does not supply an adverse buyer-side basic-assumption mistake.

B.signal: The later harm matches the warning that the camel jerks.
B.lawyer: Known or assumed risks do not support mistake rescission.

C.signal: The defect is hidden, severe, and destroys the buyer's main use.
C.lawyer: This is the best mistake-rescission scenario under Restatement §§ 152 and 154.

D.signal: The camel already delivered four years of the bought-for use.
D.lawyer: A collateral replica-template defect does not defeat the basic assumption of the sale.

goldKeys.statement: A mistake supports rescission only when the mistaken fact existed at contracting, went to a basic assumption with material adverse effect, and the party seeking rescission did not bear that risk. A known defect, a collateral side-use problem, or a hidden upside does not unlock buyer rescission.
goldKeys.trigger: A buyer seeks to rescind after discovering a post-sale fact about the thing sold.
goldKeys.unlocks: Distinguishes a hidden main-use defect from collateral or assumed-risk facts.

silverKeys.statement: On a buyer-rather-than-seller rescission call, sort each scenario by direction and purpose: buyer harmed or buyer helped, main use or side use, hidden risk or known risk. Keep the fact that damages the buyer's main expected use without repeating the warning already in the stem.
silverKeys.trigger: The call asks which later scenario best supports one named party's rescission action.
silverKeys.unlocks: The four-scenario answer array where every choice sounds like a post-sale surprise.

remediation.title: Mistake rescission: hidden main-use fact, no assumed risk
remediation.signal: A buyer wants rescission after a new fact appears.
remediation.tinyRule: Hidden main-use defect can support rescission; known risks, side uses, and hidden upside do not.
remediation.trap: Treating any surprising post-sale fact as enough.
